title: Day-2 Troubleshooting Workflow
description: Develop a systematic approach to diagnosing and resolving Kubernetes production issues using kubectl, logs, events, metrics, and common debugging patterns.

data.text: **Day-2 operations** refers to everything you do after an application is deployed and running in production. While Day-1 is about getting the application deployed, Day-2 is about keeping it healthy, performant, and up-to-date. The most critical Day-2 skill is troubleshooting: when something breaks at 2 AM, you need a repeatable, systematic approach to find and fix the problem quickly.

A good troubleshooting workflow follows a top-down approach: start from the user's experience (can they reach the app?), move through the network layer (is traffic reaching the cluster?), then the control plane (are controllers healthy?), and finally the application layer (are the Pods and containers healthy?).

terms.definition: Ongoing maintenance, monitoring, and troubleshooting of deployed applications.
A kubectl plugin and built-in command for creating debugging Pods and copying running containers.
A temporary debugging container added to a running Pod for troubleshooting.
Time-stamped records of actions and state changes in the cluster, viewable with kubectl describe.
A container termination reason indicating the container exceeded its memory limit.

data.text: When a user reports that an application is down, do not jump straight to the Pods. Start from the outside and work your way in. This systematic approach prevents you from chasing symptoms instead of root causes.

items: Check external access: Is the Ingress or LoadBalancer reachable? Is DNS resolving correctly?
Verify Services: Do the Services exist? Do they have endpoints? kubectl get endpoints.
Inspect Pods: Are the Pods running? kubectl get pods -o wide shows node placement.
Read Pod logs: kubectl logs <pod> reveals application-level errors.
Describe the Pod: kubectl describe pod <pod> shows events, probe failures, and OOMKilled status.
Check node health: kubectl get nodes shows node conditions and resource pressure.
Review controller status: kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> shows Deployment health.

data.caption: A top-down troubleshooting flow for Kubernetes production issues.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[User reports issue] --> B[Check external access]
    B -->|DNS/Ingress OK| C[Check Services]
    C -->|Endpoints exist| D[Check Pods]
    D -->|Pods running| E[Check logs]
    E -->|Logs clean| F[Check node health]
    F -->|Nodes healthy| G[Check controllers]
    B -->|DNS fails| H[Fix DNS/Ingress]
    C -->|No endpoints| I[Fix Service selector]
    D -->|Pod crashloop| J[Fix container/image]
    E -->|Error in logs| K[Fix application code]

data.text: Kubernetes stores the state of your entire cluster in its API server. Almost every troubleshooting question can be answered by querying this state with kubectl. These are the commands you should know by heart.

rows: List Pods with node placement and IP addresses
Show detailed events, conditions, probe failures, and container state
View logs from a previously crashed container
View logs from a specific container in a multi-container Pod
Show recent cluster events ordered by time
List nodes with status, roles, age, and version
Show real-time CPU and memory usage (requires Metrics Server)
Watch a Deployment rollout and report status

data.text: Sometimes logs and events are not enough — you need to run commands inside a running container to inspect its state. **Ephemeral containers** are temporary debugging containers you can add to a running Pod without restarting it. They share the network and process namespace of the target container, letting you run diagnostic commands like `curl`, `netstat`, or `ps` inside the Pod's context.

data.text: Production issues tend to fall into a handful of recognizable patterns. Learning to identify these patterns quickly dramatically reduces your mean time to resolution (MTTR).

items: CrashLoopBackOff: The container starts, crashes, and Kubernetes restarts it repeatedly. Check logs, image correctness, and resource limits.
ImagePullBackOff: The container image cannot be pulled. Check image name, tag, registry credentials, and network access.
OOMKilled: The container exceeded its memory limit. Increase the memory limit or optimize the application's memory usage.
Pending Pod: The Pod cannot be scheduled. Check node resource availability, taints and tolerations, and PersistentVolumeClaim status.
Readiness probe failing: The Pod is running but not ready. Check the application's health endpoint and startup sequence.

data.title: Start with describe and events
data.text: 90% of the time, kubectl describe pod <pod> tells you exactly what is wrong. Events at the bottom of the describe output show probe failures, scheduling issues, and image pull errors without needing to guess.

data.title: Debug a failing production Pod
data.description: Practice diagnosing common Kubernetes issues using kubectl.
steps: Deploy a Pod with an intentionally wrong image tag to trigger ImagePullBackOff.
Use kubectl describe pod to find the exact error.
Fix the image tag and verify the Pod starts.
Deploy a Pod with a memory limit set too low and a stress command to trigger OOMKilled.
Use kubectl describe pod to confirm OOMKilled and kubectl logs --previous to see what happened.
Create a Deployment with a bad readiness probe path.
Verify the Pod is running but has no endpoints in the Service.
data.expectedOutcome: You can systematically diagnose ImagePullBackOff, OOMKilled, and readiness probe failures using kubectl.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Day-2 operations focus on keeping deployed applications healthy and performant.
Start troubleshooting from the outside: user, DNS, Ingress, Services, Pods, nodes.
kubectl describe pod is your most powerful diagnostic tool — check events first.
kubectl logs --previous reveals logs from crashed containers.
Ephemeral containers let you run commands inside a Pod without restarting it.
Recognize common failure patterns (CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, ImagePullBackOff) to reduce MTTR.
data.takeaway: A systematic troubleshooting workflow turns chaotic production fires into fast, repeatable diagnoses.
